lines.trans: Kostya, have you finished preparing the drinks?
Yes, all orders are already ready.
Why did Max run away from here so quickly?
He was simply in a big hurry to get to the kitchen.
It seems to me that he is behaving strangely.
Max is always a slightly strange guy.
Did he not say anything to you about me?
We spoke only about our work.
Are you definitely telling me the pure truth?
Of course, I never deceive you.
Fine, then I will ask him myself.
It is better not to disturb him right now, Vika.

meanings.note: the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order
the comparative 'быстрее', often as an order

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

examples.text: Давай работай быстрее, гости уже давно ждут заказ!
examples.trans: Come on, work faster, the guests have been waiting for their order for a long time!

meanings.en: to lead, to guide, to drive
meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to lead', forming an aspectual pair with 'повести'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Вы как маленькая себя ведёте = You're behaving like a little girl

examples.trans: You're behaving like a little girl.

examples.text: Лидия Алексеевна, успокойтесь, пожалуйста! Вы как маленькая себя ведёте.
examples.trans: Lydia Alexeyevna, calm down, please! You're behaving like a little girl.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'егда').

examples.trans: She's offended. She's always like that.

говорить.gloss: to speak, to say, to talk

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to speak', forming an aspectual pair with 'сказать'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('to speak, to talk') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to cook; to prepare', paired with 'приготовить'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to prepare') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я уже не могу готовить, стирать, убирать. Я хочу на море!
examples.trans: I can't take the cooking, washing and cleaning any more. I want to go to the sea!

meanings.note: usually the short form: я готов (m), я готова (f)
emphatic at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('? = really?, oh yeah?') (disbelief) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Declinable masculine noun meaning 'order', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('booking') (commission or reservation) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Я делаю всё точно по вашему заказу.
examples.trans: I do everything exactly according to your order.
In the kitchen they are preparing this order.

meanings.en: to finish, to end, to complete
meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (stem 'кончить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to finish', forming an aspectual pair with 'заканчивать'.

examples.trans: I want to finish what I started.

examples.text: Был неправ. Простите. Я хочу закончить начатое.
examples.trans: I was wrong. Forgive me. I want to finish what I started.

meanings.note: мне кажется = I think, it seems to me
Secondary conversational sense ('it seems, I think') (кажется as a parenthetical word) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I think I've seen you somewhere.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'of course'.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).
Secondary conversational sense ('cuisine, cooking') (русская кухня = Russian cuisine) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Three rooms and a big kitchen.
And the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'better'.
нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('onto, to; for') (+ accusative: на второй срок) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: The programme is on the website.
He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Derived masculine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'drink'.

examples.text: Ты совсем не пьёшь крепкие напитки?
examples.trans: Do you not drink strong drinks at all?
The bartender made a delicious cold beverage.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates
Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'много'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I need to do a bit of work.

examples.text: Мы даём вам ещё немного времени.
examples.trans: We are giving you a little more time.

meanings.note: used with не before the verb, or alone

examples.text: Я никогда не был на море.
examples.trans: I've never been to the sea.

examples.text: Я никогда в жизни не пробовал такой вкусной утки!
examples.trans: I have never in my life tasted such delicious duck!

meanings.note: usually in the genitive ничего, with не: ничего не осталось

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.note: + prepositional; об before a vowel: об этом

examples.text: Мне некогда об этом думать. Слишком много дел.
examples.trans: I have no time to think about that. There's too much to do.

meanings.note: Prefix 'об-' ('around, about') marks encirclement or comprehensive action (stem 'манывать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to deceive, to cheat', paired with 'обмануть'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to lie to') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Потому что она простая. Её все обманывают.
examples.trans: Because she's naive. Everybody cheats her.

meanings.note: accusative/genitive его (него after prepositions), dative ему (нему)

examples.trans: I'll be out of here in two weeks. I'll solve all your problems.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'просить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to ask', paired with 'спрашивать'.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'strange'.

examples.trans: How strange, I've heard nothing about it.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'транный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('strange, odd').
